protocol.investigation: How did selected communities in Canada around1780–1850 meet everyday needs and respond to challenges?
preparation: Provide actual source items or clearly attributed accessible written source cards from the reviewed packets. Require substantive inquiry use of the Anishinaabe/Fort William, Lake Superior Métis and Inuvialuit/Kuukpak cases, alongside selected settler comparisons; the three distinct peoples are not optional alternatives. Retain author, date, place and original-source type. Use actual public institutional accounts and selected age-appropriate original historical evidence, not fictional testimony.

Provide the actual Cary1811historical map electronically and in print with readable labels and teacher-prepared source-attributed location markers. The northern location reference is the previously reviewed NWT heritage account https://www.nwttimeline.ca/stories/inuvialuit-lifeways/ (actual Inuvialuit Lifeways body and Kuukpak object captions), locating the case broadly in the Mackenzie Delta/Western Arctic; pair this with broad globe orientation. Do not imply the southern detailed Cary base depicts the northern case. A teacher-prepared northern locator must be explicitly based on this attributed geographic reference, not an invented historical boundary. No pupil address or family history is required.

Source cards must support the selected questions. Do not invent a missing measurement, transform a report’s silence into a fact or treat two paraphrases of the same underlying source as independent evidence.
actions: Formulate at least three substantive, answerable questions within the investigation and explain why the source approach is useful. A suggested set asks how people obtained/moved food and materials; how shelter and community learning helped meet needs; and how land pressures or movement shaped a studied community’s response. Learner questions may replace these if the prepared sources genuinely support them.

Gather information for EACH chosen question from at least two distinct relevant source items. The food/material/transport question can compare reviewed Fort William and Traill accounts, supplemented by the independently attributed MNO archival research. The shelter/learning question can use period-life accounts and the1849–1850Buxton institutional accounts. For land/movement, use the actual MNO Drummond1828account and the separately authored Six Nations/Haldimand or MCFN treaty account. Keep the actual question and source relevance explicit, not a list of unrelated facts.

Organise source-labelled written notes by community, date, challenge, response and what evidence supports it. Read and interpret the selected source cards; merely hearing an adult’s answer is not the whole retained ShortResearch evidence. Compose an original summary combining at least two sources, without copying their wording.

Analyse BOTH printed and digital map views. Locate actual studied communities broadly, waterways and the relevant dated case points. Explain how the geographic information helps investigate a particular challenge or response. Construct BOTH a printed and a digital thematic map with title, labels and a key, for example showing selected documented food/transport routes or the actual dated movement between two studied places. Use only source-supported routes; a line indicating broad movement is not an exact historical travel track.

Use more than one relevant tool to interpret information: the actual thematic maps plus a comparison matrix of challenges, responses and source dates. Identify a pattern and a case that limits a generalization. The matrix is qualitative when the evidence is qualitative; no chart of incidental source-word counts is manufactured.

Evaluate selected evidence by identifying who made it, when and why, and an actual limitation: Traill’s settler standpoint, the institutional viewpoint of the Buxton account, surviving archival labels in the MNO research, or a colonial map’s omissions. Compare what a source directly records with a supported inference; perform a concrete corroboration of the Buxton1849foundation date across the actual Parks Canada designation account and Presbyterian Archives mission account. State their different perspectives and that agreement alone does not prove independent underlying records; two paraphrases of one underlying account do not count as independent corroboration.

Draw a conclusion answering the actual question about challenges AND responses, linking it to source evidence and acknowledging uncertainty. Do not infer that all communities faced identical problems, that one solution worked for everyone or that an agreement’s existence proves fair implementation.

Communicate a clear original written/visual account using accurate case-specific vocabulary and appropriate dates, place labels and source attribution. Use a suitable presentation form rather than requiring every illustrative source vocabulary item or every possible medium. Explain how evidence changed or qualified an initial idea.
protocol.positive: A coherent multi-community, dated historical inquiry actually uses First Nations, Métis AND Inuit case evidence and includes meaningful questions, relevant varied source gathering, both print/digital map analysis and construction, multiple interpretation tools, concrete source corroboration/evaluation, conclusions and original communication.
nearMiss: Copies an adult summary without consulting the selected written sources.
Asks three questions but gathers two sources only for one.
Adds routes or exact historical boundaries because a modern map looks convenient.
Constructs only a printed map while naming a digital tool.
Builds an irrelevant bar chart to make a qualitative account look quantitative.
Presents a later school policy as a1780event or all historical source judgments as neutral facts.
protocol.transfer: Investigate a new bounded question about a studied community using one fresh accessible attributed source and a changed map view. State what evidence supports the conclusion and what additional information would be needed.

performanceConditions.communities: Actual inquiry must use the reviewed First Nations, Métis AND Inuit cases, with multiple specific communities overall. Merely making a case available does not account for its use. The at-least-one Indigenous minimum in specific clauses is retained separately and does not weaken the overall expectation.
performanceConditions.sourceConsultation: At least three real questions, at least two relevant distinct source items for each; original organised written notes and two-source synthesis preserve the unchanged whole ShortResearch claim.
performanceConditions.conclusion: Supported answer about period challenges and measures, with limitations.

boundaries: Fifteen component pairs extend existing exact CA8–9contexts; no new claim, age band, guide or dependency change is proposed.

Source-fit protocols reuse the whole current generic operations with historical facts from separately reviewed knowledge cards. Neither method mastery nor one local performance automatically certifies all Canadian period knowledge.

The retained hard prerequisite closure is unchanged; for example conclusions’ quantitative data prerequisite remains a separate existing readiness issue, not a reason to add an irrelevant chart to the historical source task.
Historical source-evidence evaluation here is introductory. It does not import the later formal evidence-versus-interpretation claim or a stronger causal-strength criterion.
This is an untested authoring design and source-fit proposal, not an observed learner outcome.
